one_liner: Go Roaring bitmaps stored as one byte slice, no marshalling; beats Go roaring64 v0.6.1 FastOr, not 32-bit Go roaring.
what_it_does: sroar (Serialized Roaring Bitmaps) is a Go rewrite of Roaring bitmaps for uint64 values. The whole bitmap (key index plus containers) lives in one []uint16 that is also the serialized form: FromBuffer wraps a []byte without parsing, and ToBuffer returns the backing bytes, so a bitmap can go to disk or the network without a marshal step. The API is its own (NewBitmap, Set, Contains, And, Or, AndNot, FastOr, FastParOr, FastAnd, Rank, Select, Split, iterators), not a drop-in for RoaringBitmap/roaring or CRoaring, and the byte format is not the Roaring portable format.
how_it_is_fast: FastOr first sums per-key container cardinalities across all inputs, pre-creates every key, then lays out full 8 KiB bitmap containers before sized array containers at the tail of the buffer, so the union is written into pre-sized space with lazy cardinality and almost no allocation (9 to about 60 allocs per op, against up to 54,500 for roaring64 on census1881). Containers are array or bitmap only (no run containers), stored inline in the flat buffer; growth shifts the tail with copy (scootRight) instead of allocating new container objects.
when_to_use: Go services that persist or ship many bitmaps (posting lists, inverted indexes) and want zero-copy load from mmap or a network buffer, as Dgraph did
Unions over many 64-bit bitmaps where the Go roaring64 v0.6.1 FastOr allocated hundreds of MB per call (census1881 585 MB/op against 1.4 MB/op for sroar)
Workloads where GC pressure from many small container objects matters more than raw set-operation speed
Read-mostly bitmaps loaded with FromBuffer and queried in place
when_not_to_use: If your values fit in 32 bits: the repo's own benchmarks/roar32.txt (same FastOr real-data harness, same machine) has 32-bit Go roaring faster than sroar on 11 of 12 data sets, e.g. dimension_003 2.10 ms vs 11.66 ms and weather_sept_85_srt 0.48 ms vs 2.71 ms (derived from page data)
Run-heavy data, since there are no run containers; even against roaring64, FastOr is 1.4x to 3.8x slower on three of twelve sets (uscensus2000, weather_sept_85, census-income_srt)
When you need interoperability with CRoaring, Java or Go roaring files: the byte layout is sroar-specific and in host byte order
New projects wanting maintenance: dgraph-io/sroar was archived 2024-07-18 and this fork's last commit is 2022-05-27; the weaviate/sroar fork (234 commits, go 1.21) is the live line
When you need a C or C++ library: there is no measurement against CRoaring at all

integration.dependencies: github.com/pkg/errors at runtime; RoaringBitmap/roaring v0.6.1 and testify only for tests and benchmarks
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.16 per go.mod; uses //go:linkname to the unexported runtime.memclrNoHeapPointers and reflect.SliceHeader casts, so newer Go releases may reject or warn
integration.platforms: Any Go platform in principle; buffers are reinterpreted with unsafe casts and no endian conversion, so the serialized form is only portable between hosts of the same byte order; benchmarks only on x86-64 (Threadripper 2950X)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no internal locking, so concurrent mutation is unsafe; FastParOr runs FastOr on bitmap groups in separate goroutines and merges the results

gotchas: Memclr (exported, utils.go) passes len(b) of a []uint16 as the byte count to runtime.memclrNoHeapPointers, so it zeroes only the first half of the slice; internal callers appear to tolerate it (array containers are bounded by their stored cardinality and toBitmapContainer re-clears with copy from a zero slice), and I found no wrong result, but any outside caller of sroar.Memclr gets a half-cleared slice.

FromBuffer aliases the caller's []byte (its doc says modifying the bitmap may corrupt the buffer; use FromBufferWithCopy to write), and FastOr with a single argument returns that same bitmap rather than a copy.
Importing the package allocates a 16<<20-element []uint16 (32 MiB) global zero slice named empty.
Bitmap-container Maximum() bug reported in dgraph-io/sroar PR #33 (2023-03-13) was closed unmerged when the repo was archived; the same fix was merged as weaviate/sroar#5, not here.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick sroar over its Zig sibling zroar (same author, same serialized-Roaring design, measured against CRoaring 5.0.0) only when you are in Go and need the buffer-is-the-bitmap layout; for a measured win over a C baseline use zroar, and for maintained Go code use the weaviate/sroar fork.
verified_claims_summary: The README's 6.5x (p50, benchmarks over 1 ms) figure compares sroar FastOr on twelve Roaring real-data sets against Go RoaringBitmap/roaring roaring64 v0.6.1 on a Threadripper 2950X with an unstated Go version; the sroar column (benchmarks/sroar.txt) was re-run on 2021-12-09 while the roaring64 column (roar64.txt) dates from a 2021-05-18 run whose harness is no longer in the repo, so it is a cross-run comparison, and no C or C++ baseline was measured.
status_note: Abandoned: a 2022-05-27 fork of dgraph-io/sroar (archived 2024-07-18, go.mod still names github.com/dgraph-io/sroar) under Apache-2.0; the headline numbers are a cross-run comparison against roaring64 only, and the repo's own roar32.txt shows 32-bit Go roaring faster than sroar on 11 of 12 data sets, so treat the speedup as a fix for roaring64 v0.6.1's allocation-heavy FastOr rather than a general win; reproducing it on HEAD also needs -tags real (real_data_test.go carries a 'real' build tag the README command omits).
